utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to all. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: For the Office of the Prosecutor, Gerard Dobbyn, along with Joanna Korner and our Case Manager, Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The microphone needs to be adjusted for the Prosecutor, we can't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please, needs to be adjusted. He is very far from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There's a problem with your microphone. It's not well directed. It's not well directed. Okay. Now, if you have just a moment, please, we have a ruling. On the 4th of November, the Trial Chamber ordered that written motion be filed identifying the documents put to Branko Djeric during cross-examination which are sought for admission into evidence. On the 12th of November, the Stanisic Defence and the Zupljanin Defence, by way of e-mail to the Chamber's Legal Officer, submitted lists of documents that they sought to have admitted. It is noted that this was not done through a formal written motion as ordered. Nevertheless, in the interest of expediency, the Trial Chamber has reviewed the list submitted and will issue its ruling now. Several of the documents are already in evidence and need not to be considered by the Chamber. They are Rule 65 ter numbers 180, 606, 609, and 1229. The Chamber has reviewed the testimony of Branko Djeric and the parties' submissions as to the admissibility of the remaining Defence documents. It decides to admit into evidence as Stanisic Defence exhibits the following documents: 1D00-0496, 1D00-0507, 1D00-0515, 1D00-0552, 1D00-0769, 1D00-3812, 1D00-4266, and Rule 65 ter numbers 176, 194, 306, 932, 1285, 123 -- sorry, 1350, 1398, and 3033. The Trial Chamber does not find that the remaining documents submitted by the Stanisic Defence meet the requirements for admission through Branko Djeric, and they will not be admitted at this time. The Chamber decides to admit into evidence as Zupljanin Defence exhibits the documents numbered 2D07-0049, and 65 ter number 2673.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsels on both sides, today we are going to hear the expert witness on the Crisis Staffs, and the Chamber wonders if it would be useful to ask the parties before we bring in Mrs. Hanson to summarise in a nutshell their position on the Crisis Staffs so that we know where the parties agree on the role of the Crisis Staffs, and where they disagree, because I think this will enable us to have a more focused examination and cross-examination of this expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, although Mr. Dobbyn is actually calling Mrs. Hanson, Your Honours, it's all very well to spring that on us at 10 past 9.00 in the morning, but if we'd known about this in advance, we could have actually thought about it more carefully. I think it's not terribly helpful off the top of one's head to -- to put a position with respect to the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I would imagine that you are well prepared, then, and that you have the main points ready in your head.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, Your Honours, I'm afraid -- I mean, if we start saying something without thinking about it in advance, it becomes much longer, more diffuse, and we can certainly do it if that's what Your Honours want to do after the break. I mean, we just need time to sit down and deal with it. But, as I say, I don't think it's a terribly productive exercise just to do it off the top of one's head. Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm a bit surprised about your position, but I will take your words for it. And so the Chamber still thinks that it is a useful exercise to ask the parties to summarise their main views on the role of the Crisis Staffs because, as I said, this will enable the Chamber to ascertain where the parties agree and where they disagree so that we can focus on these points during the examination and cross-examination and also through the questions by the Judges. But if this poses a problem to you, then we would suggest that we have this exercise in the first -- after the first break. If you could get together during the break and see if you can line out just, you know, in bullet points, the three or four or five main points that you may agree or disagree on in relation to the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, is Your Honour suggesting that we should get together with the Defence and work this out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's up to you. I think it would be useful but we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, otherwise, Your Honour, how are we to know where we disagree, if you see what I mean. We can't -- at the moment, as we've said over and over again, rather, we don't actually know what the main points of disagreement are, although we can guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because we ran through the pre-trial briefs but did not find very clearly set out the parties' views on the role of the Crisis Staffs, and this is why we wanted actually to have this summarised or crystallised a bit. But let's bring in Ms. Hanson and then in the break we kindly ask you to see if you can summarise for yourself and then get together with the Defence to see if it's possible to find out where you disagree and where you agree. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, while --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, but, Your Honours, in due -- all due respect, I don't think -- I mean it makes a lot of sense what Your Honour is suggesting and I guess we should sit down with our friends from the Prosecution and discuss the matter, but it's -- I don't think it's realistic that we can do it in 20 minutes and be prepared to make a submission for Your Honours. As Ms. Korner rightly said, we should have put on notice then we could have used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To be honest --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To be honest, Mr. Zecevic, the Chamber had expected that you would have done this anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, but, Your Honours, with all due respect, we ask for more time in the preparation of this case and we were rushed into the beginning of this case by Your Honours' decision. We said we were not prepared. Therefore, I -- with all due respect, I decline that we should have done anything more than we are doing right now because we are working around the clock, Your Honours. And it's physically not possible for us or the Prosecutor's Office to even engage into the things which I suggested should have been done in the pre-trial phase. That is why the Defence of Stanisic insisted that we prolong the start of the trial for one month where we -- we guaranteed to the Trial Chamber that this one month will help shorten the trial for five months. That wasn't accepted, and I -- I mean, we are here where we are now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is a good statement. We are where we are. That's always nice to know. As a sailor and a navigator, I certainly appreciate the notion that you have to know where you are. But, Mr. Zecevic, the Chamber did whatever we felt we could do by postponing the testimony of Mrs. Hanson until you have had sufficient time to familiarise yourself with it. This was the whole exercise about the ban and I really don't think that the parties getting together for a couple of hours at some point to just sit down and discuss where you disagree and agree on the role of the Crisis Staffs would have been such a tremendous effort by the parties. So, you know, I'm not blaming you or Mr. Pantelic or Ms. Korner for not having done it. It's just that we would have expected that this would be a very natural thing to do, to actually get together and see where we are in relation to role of the Crisis Staffs. Especially because, as I said, neither of the parties have lined out very clearly in their pre-trial briefs what they think about the role of the Crisis Staffs. But be that as it may, I mean, we are, as you said, where we are, and let's have Mrs. Hanson brought in, and if possible, in the break you can get together, you can have -- we can have an extended break if that's acceptable to you. But I really think it makes very good sense to do just what the Chamber has proposed because it helps understand better where you stand -- the positions of the parties against each other and it helps the Chamber to understand what to look for in her testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, all we are saying is, we certainly could have done it. We could have done it yesterday afternoon, but Your Honours didn't tell us this is what you wanted. So, I appreciate what Your Honours say, that you expected it to happen. Your Honours know that there have been difficulties getting agreement on anything, so that's the situation. But if in future Your Honours want something like this, perhaps if you would be kind enough to let us know at the end of the previous session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but again, especially when we deal with experts, I think it would make very good sense for both parties anyway always to just pick up the phone, you know, a couple of days in advance and perhaps arrange for a meeting and take an hour or two to sit down and go through the expert's report in order to find out where the points of contention are. And if we hadn't made ourselves very clear on this aspect, then it's a good time to do it now. And so for the remaining experts, the Chamber would expect the parties to be ready to line out their positions prior to the expert's arrival. So we have Christian Nielsen next week and we have a couple of other experts coming further down the road, and when the Defence cases are going to start, the Defence will also bring their experts, and so there again we expect the parties to be able to summarise their positions before the experts come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just before the witness does come in, I'd just like to clarify, I did request -- seek leave to spend two hours with this witness, I just wanted to check before she came in that that was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have one and a half hour, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: That had been the request when she was going to be called the first, which, I believe, was a couple of months ago. From that time, having spent more time speaking to Ms. Hanson, going through documents, we feel that two hours would be on the safe side. Certainly I would try to get it done within an hour and a half, but seeking an extra half-hour was really to be on the safe side to try to get through this properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, are you asking for an extra half-hour on top of the two hours that you have asked for previously?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honours. We had asked for a total of two hours, it's an extra half-hour on top of the one and a half hours that had been asked for some weeks ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning, madam. Will you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Hanson, you have been called as an expert in this trial and an expert for the Prosecution, I should add. And the Chamber has granted the Prosecution a total of two hours to take you through your expert report which we have read and accepted as an expert report, and after that the Defence teams have asked for altogether six hours for their cross-examination. You have testified already in a number of cases so you know the game. I don't need to instruct you further on that. But before we proceed, I would like for the record, would you state your name and the your date of birth and your current occupation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dorothea Curtis Hanson. Date of birth, August 10th, 1962. I'm an analyst in the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I pass the word to Mr. Dobbyn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry to interrupt. Your Honours, I understand you said that the Trial Chamber have read and accepted as an expert report. I thought the ruling was that the Trial Chamber will decide on the acceptance of the expert report only after the cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I said that we have accepted the report as an expert report. The question of admission is a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have not admitted the report but we have accepted the report and Mrs. Hanson's status as an expert. So that before she begins to testify, she knows and you know that she will be testifying as an expert with the qualities that come with that qualification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm so sorry. Mr. Zecevic reminded me that that had been your ruling. It was something I meant to raise because it's the same problem as with the 92 ter witnesses. If the report is not accepted as an exhibit and has to wait until after cross-examination, then we don't know, from examination-in-chief, how much we have to go through. That's the problem

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We will MFI the expert report at this time and then come back to the final ruling once Mrs. Hanson's testimony has been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Before we start, can I just ask you that when you're responding to my questions that you speak slowly and also observe a gap between my questions and your answers just so the translators are able to keep up with us. First of all, I don't intend to go through your CV in any sort of detail but I just want to briefly highlight some of your work since you've been with the OTP. And is it the case, Ms. Hanson, that you've been employed by the OTP as an analyst since 1999?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in 2005, you testified as an expert in the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Did you also testify earlier this year as an expert in the Bosnian state court in the K lickovic case?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If we could show 65 ter 10019. And if I could also have Madam Usher's assistance, I prepared a binder for Ms. Hanson, and this contains a copy of Ms. Hanson's report as well as documents that will be shown, used with Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Hanson on the screen in front of you and also in the binder, is this a copy of your expert report that you've prepared in this case?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in the course of preparing that report, what were the source materials that you used?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I used the documents in the possession of the OTP, documents of the Crisis Staffs, Municipal Crisis Staffs themselves, as well as documents of other Bosnian Serb state organs, institutions, and individuals such as Assembly minutes, minutes of the government, some contemporary records in open source. But mostly it was the documents generated by the Crisis Staffs themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And were you working with the original B/C/S documents in any cases?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, almost exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Do you read and understand B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what about Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, I understand we have a couple of corrections that you would like to make to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So if we could please go to page 28 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I understand that the B/C/S version is fine.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise for this. It was -- at one point the report had been -- every time Variant A and B was -- appeared, it was replaced by the full name of the document and it should not be here in Karadzic's quotation where he --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if we could just stop, just to get it on screen. We are looking at paragraph 63, which it is at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It's the very last line. He says: "You will remember," and here the text reads, "instructions for the organisation and activities of organs of the Serbian people," on to the next page to the end of "under extraordinary circumstances." That's the full title of Variant A and B, and here he just says -- in the original he says: "Variant A and Variant B." I have the correct quotation earlier in the report and I apologise that slipped in there. The correct version is on page 10, paragraph 20. So here it should simply read Variant A and Variant B.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If we could next go on to page 36 in the English and page 38 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for interruption. We have problem with the e-court. Actually, we have problem with the screens so we cannot follow and our client also are not able to follow. So please can you fix it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have the same. The screens are blinking all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And so do we. We are being told that the technician is on his way to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have the suggestion that we could perhaps use the witness's copy on the ELMO to go until this is resolved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The problem is that we are not very good at reading B/C/S and so if we show the English version, the accused won't be able to read it, and if we show the B/C/S version, then we won't be able to understand it, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours. I think it would be preferable perhaps if we could wait until the technician could sort this out. We do have several documents to go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, I understand that the problem has been temporarily solved, so we may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Hanson, sorry for the delay. We were looking at paragraph 80 of your report, and I understand that you have a correction to make there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. I made a poor choice of words when I say that the police were financed in the municipality. I really meant to say materially supported, given equipment, uniforms by the municipal authorities, but not that they were the sole source of -- not that the municipal authorities were the sole source of finance for the police. So materially supported is what I should have written.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. And with those two changes in mind, Your Honours, I'd ask that this expert report be MFI'd at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So ordered. Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P434, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, just to be clear, does your -- just to be clear, Ms. Hanson, does your area of expertise include the structure and function of the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: So it's limited solely to the Bosnian Serb Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: As a specialised area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on now to a couple of questions about the origins of the Crisis Staffs. And can you tell us, Ms. Hanson, were the Bosnian Serb Crisis Staffs that were operating from 1991 an entirely new phenomenon or did they have some kind of legal precedent?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: There was a legal precedent, two perhaps, in the form of one -- a collective municipal Presidency. Many -- the constitution of Bosnia foresaw that if the Municipal Assembly could not meet, there would be a collective Presidency. There was also the idea of the -- from the communist era, the All People's Defence committees which were a larger group to include all the leaders in the municipality including the party leadership, military police. This was to allow some kind of defence to continue even when communication was lost with the central organs. That was a legacy of the partisan area. Nowhere in the legislation have I seen the term "Crisis Staff." But I know that people have testified in the past that the term was known. I do not claim that the term was invented here. Crisis Staffs could be apparently some ad hoc small groups to deal with specific crises, but I see that the legislative origin in the municipal collective presidencies and the All People's Defence committees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can you explain briefly to the Court how the SDS Crisis Staffs came to be formed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: They were formed on the basis of instructions dated the 19th of December, also known as the A and B instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Under these instructions, what was the role of the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The role of the Crisis Staff was to organise the defence of the Serb -- interests of the Serbian people to perform essentially as a shadow government creating -- undertaking preparations for establishing Serbian municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Was there a specific goal that the Crisis Staffs had?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: To establish Serbian municipalities and municipal organs. To be the organs of power in a Serbian municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could we call up now, please, Exhibit P69.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, this is already in evidence and it is a copy of the Variant A and B instructions. And it's in tab 1 of your binder. Thank you. Now, Ms. Hanson, we can see that these instructions are from the SDS Main Board. They have a copy number 93, and the heading is: "Instructions for the organisation and operation of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in emergency conditions." Now, Ms. Hanson, the copy number 93, can you tell us how many municipalities there were in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I believe about 107, less than 100. Between 100 and 110. I think it was 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: What was the highest number of any copies of the Variant A and B instructions that were found in the OTP's collections?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And what inference, if any, do you draw from the numbering of these A and B instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Different numbers have been found in different municipalities and my inference is that it was one per -- one copy per municipality was numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could we now please go to page 2 in both the English and B/C/S of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in particular I'm looking at item 4, Ms. Hanson, at the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Item?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Item 4.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It calls to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Hanson, if we could wait for it, to make sure it's up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: The English is not matching the B/C/S. No, it's not the same. The B/C/S says: "Call and proclaim an Assembly of the Serbian people in the municipality made up of deputies from the ranks of the Serbian people in the Municipal Assembly."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And we're --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Or did you want the --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: -- still waiting for page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's numbered -- it's page 3 of the document itself that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Okay. We have it now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. That's what you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Item 4 reads, Ms. Hanson: "In order to ensure the consistent and timely implementation, tasks, measures and other activities shall be set forth in two variants, A and B, and at two levels."

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I was ahead of you there. Yes, Variant A is for the municipalities where the Serbs are in a majority. Variant B, where they are in a minority. And the two levels, the first is the initial preparations, and the second is the actual take-over of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, did the instructions say anything about the composition of the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. They spelled out the composition. The president of the Crisis Staff -- well, the composition is slightly different between Variant A and Variant B, but the purpose is very much the same, that the municipal leaders -- the Serb -- the leading Serbs in the municipal authorities are to be part of the Crisis Staffs. The president of the Municipal Assembly, or the president of the SDS Municipal Board in the case of B, to be the commander of the Crisis Staff to include the head of the police station or the commander of the police or the SDS candidate for that position. Members of the Main Board of the SDS, delegates to the National Assembly of the SDS, all those who carry some function in the municipal -- in the municipality, the head of the municipal staff of the TO, the head of the -- the secretary of the Municipal Secretariat of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And just to be clear, Ms. Hanson, was it foreseen in the instructions that there would be police representation under both Variant A and Variant B municipalities on the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on from the actual instructions themselves now to look at the Municipal Boards acting upon instructions. Now, what did your examination of the materials show with regards to how this report was distributed and to whom it was distributed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: There -- I have evidence that it was distributed on the 20th of December, or thereabouts, and was received by the Municipal Boards or municipal presidents and implemented. There are many instances of the SDS Municipal Boards, in the last days of December, receiving and implementing these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could look at an example of that. If we could show 65 ter 398.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this is in tab 2 of your binder, Ms. Hanson. And this document -- these are abridged minutes from a meeting of the Prijedor SDS Municipal Board from the 27th of December, 1991. We'll just wait for that to come up on the screen. Okay. If we could look at point 1. Sorry, at the bottom of the page on the English. This says: "Simo Miskovic, president of the Prijedor SDS Municipal Board, gave a brief introduction. President Miskovic then read out the instructions forwarded to the Prijedor SDS Municipal Board by the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we could now go to the next page on the English, remaining on the same page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: "Since there are only two versions, only version 2 which is relevant for Prijedor municipality was read out. Having read out all the items in sections A and B of version 2, Miskovic explained what had been done so far with respect to the instructions." Now, Ms. Hanson, having read over that portion, do you have any comment to make about that and how that is relevant to implementation?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It appears that Miskovic received a copy of A and B and is implementing it in the municipality. He -- as recorded in the minutes, they do seem to have switched Variant A and B, level 1 and 2, but the usage and, moreover, the steps taken afterwards including forming a Crisis Staff make it clear to me at least that it's a question of the A and B document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, remaining on page 1 of the B/C/S and page 2 of the English, another portion that I'd like to read to you, and this is towards the bottom of the page in English, and likewise in the B/C/S. "Reasons and functions were stated for establishment of the Municipal Crisis Staff and local staffs on territory of the municipality. The decision was made to introduce around-the-clock duty in the SDS offices according to the chart which had been established: Prijedor 2 on 27 December, Cirkin Polje on 28 December, et cetera." Now, Ms. Hanson, these points refer to forming a Crisis Staff in Prijedor and introducing duty watches.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Are these continue with 19 December instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, the interpreters ask that you put your headphones on so that you can receive their observations about the speed in which you speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. My Case Manager had just pointed that out to me and I'll certainly keep them on now. Now if we could go over to page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And you'll see at point 2 at the top of the page, Ms. Hanson, it sets out the composition of the Prijedor Crisis Staff. How did this composition compare to that set out in the 19 December instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It is consistent with the 19 December instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd seek to tender this document at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be Exhibit P435.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could we now call up 65 ter 3430.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Which is tab 3 of your binder, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I have a small window on my screen, does everyone have that? Blocking part of the document. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: This document, Ms. Hanson, is entitled: "Conclusions of SDS Zvornik Municipal Board Meeting Held on 22 December 1991." I'll just wait a moment for --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It's not a problem, I have the original here but -- I have the original. I can check it on the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, do you see any relationship between this document and the 19 December instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I do, indeed. I note that it's dated the 22nd of December, shortly after the distribution of the A and B document. The first item, "Round-the-clock duty," matches the A and B instructions. The Crisis Staff is chosen with the municipal president or -- I'm sorry, I can't confirm Grujic's position at the moment. He is named as komandant. The next person mentioned is the deputy at the Bosnian Serb Assembly. A co-ordinator with the SDA is also part of the A and B instructions. Item 5, "Calling a Municipal Assembly," is also part of the A and B instructions. So I find it entirely consistent. Yes, he is president of the SDS, not of Municipal Assembly, Grujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that this be tendered at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P436, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could we look next at 65 ter 3431.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this is at tab 4 of your binder, Ms. Hanson. And this is a decision regarding the formation of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik, and it's dated 27 December 1991. Now, in particular, could you look at the preamble, which is on the right -- the top paragraph on the right-hand column of the English page, and could you tell us if there's anything of significance in that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. The preamble cites explicitly the A and B. It says that: "This decision is based on Article 4 of the instructions of the organisation and activities of the organs of the Serbian people in BiH in extraordinary circumstances from 19 December 1991." So not only have they received the A and B and are implementing it, but they are citing it as the legal basis for their actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P437, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And finally on this topic, if we could pull up 65 ter 1496.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: This is in tab 5 of your binder, Ms. Hanson. This is a transcript from the 50th Session of the Republika Srpska Assembly, held on 15th, 16th April 1995. And we are just waiting for it to come up on the screen, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 306 of the English. Page 278 in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, I particularly want to focus on a quote that is about halfway down the page on the English, about a third of the way in B/C/S. And this quote states: "At the moment the war began, in the municipalities where we were in the majority, we had municipal power, held it firmly, controlled everything. In the municipalities where we were in the minority, we set up secret government, Municipal Boards, Municipal Assemblies, presidents of Executive Boards. You all remember, the A and B Variants." Now, Ms. Hanson, can you tell us who is speaking?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And can you explain the significance of this quote?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: In the Assembly, they were, at the moment, debating something about the army and he -- this is in 1995. He is looking back to the outbreak of the war and he is recalling the A and B Variants, reminding the deputies, You all remember the A and B and how it enabled us to set up secret governments and hold power.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd seek to tender this at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be Exhibit P438.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'd like to move now to the section in your report, Ms. Hanson, starting at page 12. It's headed: "From party organ to municipal government, January to April 1992." Now, at the time that they were formed, were the SDS Crisis Staffs public? Were they public bodies in the sense that the general public was aware of their existence?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: No, they were not. They were secret organs within the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And in your report you describe the evolution or change in the character of the Crisis Staffs from January to April 1992. Could you briefly summarise what happened over that period?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: This is the period when the SDS at the top level is similarly forming state organs, transforming the party into -- transforming the organs of the party into the organs of the Bosnian Serb state. And as more concrete measures were taken at the republican level, so also we see the Crisis Staffs by the end of this period, by April 1992, they are no longer secret party organs. They are public organs declaring themselves to be the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we could look at 65 ter 920 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this is in tab 6 of your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And can we go to page 22 in the English, page 39 in the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, this is a relatively lengthy quote. It's about halfway down the page in the English. It's on much of the page of the B/C/S, so I'll read through it and try not to go too fast. Continues partway through the second line of the, I believe, third full paragraph. "This will be very soon. We can form whatever we want. There are reasons why this could happen in two or three days. Such are the forecasts but I cannot tell you the reasons now. At that moment, all the Serbian municipalities, both the old ones and the newly established ones, would literally assume control of the entire territory of the municipality concerned." Continues on: "Then at a given moment, in the next three or four days, there will be a single method used and you will be able to apply it in the municipalities you represent, including both things that must be done, as well as how to do them. How to separate the police force, take the resources that belong to the Serbian people, and take command. The police must be under the control of the civilian authority. It must obey it. There's no discussion about that. That's the way it must be. I think we shall hear it today in the form of instructions at the Deputies' Club." Ms. Hanson, can you tell us who is speaking here and what the significance of this passage is?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It's Radovan Karadzic speaking. What we see in the Assembly sessions by the end of March is an eagerness to seize control on the ground. Some of the municipalities or representatives are saying, We are more than ready, just give us the order. Karadzic here is saying, You will get instructions, it will be the same instructions for everywhere, but it will be secret. That is in the Deputies' Club, not here in the Assembly, and we will take over the municipalities, take over the police -- that is, form our own police. So they are getting ready for the final take-over, and, as I say, some municipalities are champing at the bit and begging for instructions, begging for the sign to take over. Others apparently need to be brought up to speed. But it is being direct -- they are waiting from the word from on top, and Karadzic is going to give them the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I seek to tender this, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P439, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can we now move on to tab 7 in your binder, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we could call up 65 ter 2744.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: This is a press release of the National Security Council. And it's dated 4 April 1992. Ms. Hanson, can you explain what the significance of this press release is?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: As you can see, it's from the Council for National Defence or Security, National Security, and it is issued by Karadzic as the president of the National Security Council, not as the president of the SDS, which I'd see as part of this pattern from moving from party organ to state organs. And in the last paragraph he calls for the activation of Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Just to, sorry, stop you there for a second. Could we go to page 2 in the English and I believe the passage you are talking about is in the last paragraph in the English there, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, if you could please continue on with what that paragraph talks about.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: "Crisis Staffs in those area should be activated and the Serbian People's Territorial Defence, civilian protection and reserve police raised primarily for the purpose of maintaining order, peace and safety of civilians of all nationalities." So although we saw Karadzic as president of the SDS ordering the formation of Crisis Staffs in December 1991, now at the beginning of April 1992 as president of the National Security Council, he is calling for activation of Crisis Staffs in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And could I tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P440, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on with a few questions about the document known as the 26 April instructions, Ms. Hanson. Now, as the Crisis Staffs came out into the open, did they receive any direction from the republican government as to how they should operate?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. The National Security Council received a report on the work of Crisis Staffs, discussed the need for instructions, and on the 26th of April, Branko Djeric, as president of the government, issued the extract for instructions for the work of Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And could we call up please Exhibit P70, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this is tab 8 in your binder, Ms. Hanson. And is this the document that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: We see that this is headed: "Extract from the instructions for the work of Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people and municipalities," and I'm just waiting for it to come up. Now I'd like to go through a few of these specific instructions, Ms. Hanson. If we could look at item 1, this is on page 1 both English and B/C/S. "In wartime conditions, the Crisis Staff shall take over all the prerogatives and functions of Municipal Assemblies when they are not in a position to meet." Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: That means that the Crisis Staffs are the highest municipal authority. They are to replace the Assembly as a smaller collective body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Moving on to item 2, this set us out the composition of the Crisis Staffs. Now, is this composition consistent with that set out in the 19 December instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It's consistent with the 19 December instructions. It is a little more detailed for some of the more specific municipal duties towards the end, the food supplies, war crimes and so on, but it's consistent with the tasks set out also in the -- not just the composition of the Crisis Staffs but also the tasks as set out in the 19 December instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And does this again include a representative of the police --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: -- being on the Crisis Staff. Now looking at item 3, this states: "The Crisis Staff shall co-ordinate governmental functions for the purpose of the defence of territory, safety of the population and its property, establishment of authority and organisation of all other aspects of life and work. Through its co-ordination efforts, the Crisis Staff shall create the conditions for the Municipal Executive Board to exercise legal executive power, manage the economy, and other aspects of life." Now, can you comment on that particular paragraph, Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It shows that the Crisis Staff is given a fairly wide tasking of co-ordinating the authorities. So it's a co-ordinating body that is responsible for making sure the municipality is running, including the defence of the territories and everything else, all areas of life and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I'll move on now to item 6. This states: "The work of the Crisis Staff shall be based on the provisions of the constitution and the law, and on the decisions of the Assembly, the Presidency, and the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Can you comment on that article?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes. It says that the Crisis Staff is clearly supposed to be part of the Serbian -- Bosnian Serb state system, is to base its work on the decisions at the republican level and therefore is the legal municipal authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Can we move to page 2 of the English, remaining on page 1 of B/C/S, and look at paragraph or item 11. And this states that the: "The Crisis Staff shall be obliged to gather information on the situation in the field, and notify and consult the competent authorities in Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina, i.e., commissioners of the government appointed for the areas and regions especially threatened by war." Now, can you explain something about the role of the commissioner.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, we see the commissioner for the first time in these instructions. We see them more in the later decisions on the municipal organs, but essentially the commissioner is to make the link between the republican level and municipal level even closer and tighter. He is somebody appointed at the republican level to go to the municipality, get information on the situation there, and pass on the directives and policies of the republican level, and then report back to the republican level on events in the municipality and raise the municipal concern. So he is a personal link but conveying the policies and instructions and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally on this document, I'd like to look at item 14. This states: "The Crisis Staff shall make decisions and hold sessions in the presence of all its members, keep official records of proceedings, issue written decisions, and prepare weekly reports submitted to the regional and state organs of the Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina." And can you comment on that, Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: They are tasked to report to the regional and the republican level, which once again indicates their role in the Bosnian Serb state and their position in the hierarchy below the republican level. I would also note, "make decisions in the presence of all of its members," we'll see this later, that it's a collective body that reaches a collective decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this has been marked for identification. I'd seek to tender it at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Hanson, according to the instructions we've just looked at, how did the role and the operation of --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we just have the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Exhibit P70.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, it wasn't in the transcript, that is why I -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please announce it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The document will retain its P70 number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, according to these instructions, how did the role and operation of the Crisis Staffs at the municipal level compare to the operation of the government at the republican level?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: At this point you have the National Security Council and the government operating very similarly as a collective emergency body, bringing together the party, the police, the army, the leadership of that at a republican level and the Crisis Staff mirroring it at the municipal level, bringing together all of the leaders of the forces on the ground, the party, the government, to co-ordinate their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. So having looked at the 26 April instructions now, I'd like to turn and ask you some questions about Crisis Staffs whether they actually received and acted upon these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And for Your Honours and co-counsel and my learned colleagues, I'm referring to paragraph 36 of Ms. Hanson's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, in the course of reviewing the OTP's collection of documents, were you able to establish whether the Municipal Crisis Staffs actually received and acted upon these instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have found several indications that they were received and implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could I call up Exhibit P179.9.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this is in tab 9 of your binder, Ms. Hanson. It's the decision on the organisation and work of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality. You see this is dated May 1992. Ms. Hanson, to what extent, if at all, does the wording in this document reflect that of the 26 April instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Some of the articles of the Prijedor decision are almost literal transcriptions of the 26 April instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 2 of both the English and B/C/S. And look at Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this states: "The Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality is being established for the purpose of co-ordinating the functions of government, defending municipal territory, providing security for the population and their property, establishing power and authority, and organising all other aspects of life and work." Now, is this consistent with what was contained in the 26 April instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's consistent with item 3 of the earlier instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And if we could turn to Article 4 now, this is the same page in English and page 3 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Dobbyn, it's 10.25. At an appropriate point you can --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I just have perhaps two questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now this article, Ms. Hanson, sets out the composition of the Prijedor Crisis Staff, and again, was this consistent with the April instructions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's consistent with item 2 of the April instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. So, Ms. Hanson, what does this document indicate to you, at least with regards to whether the instructions were being acted upon in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It indicates that me that they were received and acted upon in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And we could break at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do Your Honours want to have a longer break so that we can see if we can reach any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What about 45 minutes, would that be okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- I don't know whether we are still having some technical problems but have the parties -- I assume the parties have been productive during the break and have something to inform the Chamber as to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we did meet with our colleagues from Defence over the break. With regards to what the Trial Chamber has requested, a summary of our position with regards to the Crisis Staffs and any points of agreement or disagreement, what I can say is that the Prosecution's position regarding the Crisis Staffs themselves is set out in the executive summary of Ms. Hanson's report. This is at page 3, and it's very succinct and probably clearer than I could do it myself, shorter and clearer than I could do it. We talked about points of agreement and disagreement, what we -- effectively the position we came to, through my understanding from the discussions, is that the major points of contention that we have with Defence on the role of the Crisis Staff or the issue of Crisis Staffs is firstly, the legality of the establishment of the Crisis Staffs, and secondly, the conclusions that our expert, Ms. Hanson, draws in her report. I think those are the two points where we have the issues. And I'm sure my colleagues will correct me if I'm wrong on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which conclusions in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I think it's many of the conclusions. It would really be the thrust -- much of the thrust of the whole of the report. But perhaps my colleagues could be more specific, if they are able, about the conclusions that they do disagree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is correct. We met and we discussed. You will remember, Your Honours, that we -- that we objected to the qualifications of this expert, as number one. We say that this expert is an employee of the Office of the Prosecutor and that her expertise basically amounts to the submission in support of the case of the Prosecution. What we are saying is that the expert is using the material, the factual material, on a highly selective and biased way, and we say that due to this fact and the fact that the expert witness does not have expertise for this kind of expert report, all the conclusions from this -- from her report are basically flaw. In that respect, we -- we certainly, as my colleague said, we certainly oppose that the conclusion that the Crisis Staff were illegal, secret bodies created by SDS and so on and so on, and we intend to cross-examine the witness on this basis. And we have enough documents to support our position and we are sure that we will be able to -- to establish that either in our cross-examination or within our Defence case, at the end of the case. So I don't know how helpful we were, but we definitely agreed that it would take us much longer time in order to achieve some kind of stipulation on the -- on the wording of this document, or in general positions. I mean, we can't do this in such a short period of time, I am afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic, and thank you, Mr. Dobbyn. It seems to me that there are a couple of issues that spring to mind based on the evidence that we have heard so far from other witnesses, which I thought are essential to understanding the expert report and which I thought also would be relevant to put to her when she comes back in the stand. One issue is the issue of the degree of co-ordination between the Crisis Staff and the army, and between the Crisis Staff and the paramilitary groups. There's a -- Ms. Hanson is not very clear in her report about these issues, and so there is obviously something that needs to be clarified with her. The other issue is the evidence that we have been given about the lifespan of the Crisis Staffs because we have had evidence to suggest that at one point the Crisis Staffs were simply not performing the way they were supposed to function, and that, therefore, the Serbian leadership wanted them demolished and replaced by another body, the war commissions or the War Presidencies which were easier to control from the top. And this is another issue which Ms. Hanson does not deal with very clearly. So here is also an area that I think would have been considered as useful to explore with the expert. And so I was also - how can I say it? - fishing for -- trying to find out if the parties have any positions about these matters and possibly other matters, but, you know, going into the details of the report, are there issues where the parties agree. For instance, do you agree that the Crisis Staffs at one point simply became so unruly and uncontrollable that they had to be dismantled and replaced by something else, is that a point agreement or disagreement between the parties? Do you agree or disagree on the degree -- on the level of control or co-ordination between the Crisis Staffs and the armed forces? So these were points that I was hoping we could perhaps have clarified. But now the Chamber has given some indication as to what we think are matters to be explored with the expert witness, and so I see no better solution than to just bring her in and continue. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the record, the understanding of Zupljanin Defence regarding the issue of Crisis Staff is as follows, just in a few points: The part of Prosecution theory with regarding to creation of Republika Srpska is that Republika Srpska and all its organs are non-legitimate. Contrary to this position of the Prosecution, the Defence is of the opinion, and this is our position, that Republika Srpska was formed fully in accordance with the right of people for [indiscernible] and also in accordance with the general principles of public international law, which, during the period of 1992, at the start of international mediation in this process, was finalised by the adopting of another source of international public law which is the Dayton Peace Accord. And finally, we have a Bosnia-Herzegovina in this stage, like a state internationally recognised but with certain specifics. And these specifics are like, one used to say that the devil is in details, is that practically on the basis of two entities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, one of which is Republika Srpska, is a full legitimate process. Of course, Defence is not challenging undisputed facts, of course, in various cases where certain crimes occurred for no -- by known or unknown perpetrators. This is a part of individual criminal responsibility of these people. However, in light of the issue of Crisis Staff, the OTP is -- has its theory of joint criminal enterprise where the certain segments of Republika Srpska, I would say, society or government, were taking certain part. Politicians, army, police, and other components. We strongly oppose this theory and this is the Defence case that we are going to present and we are going challenge all Prosecution submissions. In addition to that, my personal opinion is that not only this case, but in various cases within this Tribunal, we are actually to some extent wasting time with this political framework which is posed by Prosecution in presenting of its theory. And that's why we have to deal with political aspects, with the origins of Crisis Staff, with the roles, et cetera. But the main point for Zupljanin Defence is the particular and specific position of Mr. Zupljanin in his function as the chief of SJB Banja Luka, and particular CSB, sorry, Banja Luka, and particular relations with local police stations in regard to his mens rea and with regard to his personal knowledge of what actually happened in various locations, and this vice-versa relation. So that's, in short, is the position of the Zupljanin Defence. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. The idea was that we will now proceed and we will go on until 12.30 and then have a 20-minute break. Before we bring in Ms. Hanson, I have been notified by the French interpretation booth that since we all attend these hearings in this trial in English, it is simply that the parts of the documents - and I'm looking at you Mr. Dobbyn - are read out so fast that the French interpreters have no chance of following because they don't have the documents and they have to wait for the documents to come on the screen. So to the extent in which you will be reading passages from document, then make eye contact with the French booth if you can see them and make sure that -- or even listen to the French, if you can, make sure that they can follow. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought, may I ask for -- just for five minutes at the end of the day to raise one matter that came out of one of your rulings last Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hanson. When we left off, you had been talking about the establishment and the evolution of Municipal Crisis Staffs. Now I'd just like to ask you a couple of questions about regional Crisis Staffs. First of all, if I could ask you now, apart from Municipal Crisis Staffs, were Crisis Staffs also established at the regional level?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And do you address this in any detail in your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Not in detail because the documentary record is so unbalanced. There's a great many documents from the ARK, from the Krajina and so few from other regions that I don't feel -- I don't feel I can draw any firm conclusions on what was a pattern for regional Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: From the documents that you have been able to review, can you explain what the role of the regional Crisis Staff was?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It was similar at a regional level to the role of the Municipal Crisis Staff; that is, it was a small collective body acting in the name of the regional Assembly and similarly bringing together the regional leaders of the party, the regional government, the military, and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And did the regional Crisis Staffs play any sort of role between the municipal level and the republican government?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Yes, we see them passing on instructions from the regional level to the -- from the republican level through the region to the municipal level and implementing policies set by the republican level and informing the municipal levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to show you one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: If I can call up 65 ter 147.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: This is in tab 10 of your binder, Ms. Hanson. I'm just waiting for the document to come up. Now, Ms. Hanson, can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It's the decision on the formation of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And under point 1, we can see the composition of this Crisis Staff. And can you say how the membership of this Crisis Staff compares to the composition of Municipal Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: It is very congruent to that composition. If you notice there are military members, Lieutenant-Colonel Sajic, General Talic, a mayor. There are members of the Main Board of the SDS, Kupresanin, Radic, Vukic. Vukic is also a member of the Executive Board of the SDS. So you have those leaders who are tied to the republican centre as well as the military, and then under number 10, Zupljanin of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to tender this document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, it will be Exhibit P441.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: At this point, Ms. Hanson, I'd like to turn to the question of War Presidencies and war commissions, which are addressed in your report, and in your report you talk about these War Presidencies and war commissions. Can you explain what the difference or what the relationship was between Crisis Staffs, War Presidencies, and war commissions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: They represent essentially the same organ. We never have them operating in one municipality at the same time. It's either a Crisis Staff or a War Presidency or a war commission. What we see is in May 1992, the republican level taking further measures to establish their laws, their state institutions, and to assert control over the municipal organs that they've already created. So they are formalising the status of Crisis Staffs by sending instructions. And then 31 May, the Presidency forms -- orders the formation of Municipal War Presidencies to replace the Crisis Staffs. But the formation and the taskings are essentially the same, and indeed, we see an emphasis on the continuity between them. We see Crisis Staffs saying, Well, we are supposed to be War Presidencies but we are still calling ourselves Crisis Staffs, or, oops, Today we are a War Presidency. So they are essentially the same organs but with more explicit instructions on their formation and more explicit ties to the republican level as War Presidencies and war commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Are you aware or have you found if there was any particular reason or particular need to make this change from Crisis Staffs to war commissions?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: Well, it was Crisis Staffs, then War Presidencies and then war commissions. The commissions appear to be in those places where the municipal organs were functioning the worst, the weakest, and the commissioner had -- was delegated by the republican Presidency to go to those municipalities and get things organised. But we don't see commissions everywhere, by a long shot. The explicit -- I haven't seen an explicit explanation of why the change other than, as I say, making it more -- simply legislating it more, giving a legal basis for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Now, on the ground, to the person, the average person in the street or -- was there any clear understanding of any distinction between these different bodies?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: I have not seen such -- evidence of such a distinction being made.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could I call up at this point 65 ter 2627.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And this is at tab 126 your report, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you moving on to something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: No, this is still the same topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: And can you tell us what this document is, Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON
utterances.text: This is an instruction apparently from the ARK Crisis Staff to the municipalities, dated 11 June, so I take it to be having received and now passing on the 31 May Presidency decision on the formation of War Presidencies, because it's saying -- ordering the -- specifying the composition of War Presidencies, that is Crisis Staffs. It shows that they are clearly interchangeable. The Municipal Crisis Staff, that is the War Presidency, and then lists the formation which is consistent with the formation we've seen so far of Crisis Staffs. And it says that -- in the text, the War Presidency, that is the Crisis Staff, will lead All People's Defence in the territory of the municipality. So it ties it all the way back to the idea of the All People's Defence committees. But it clearly shows that War Presidencies and Crisis Staffs are essentially interchangeable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Could I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit P442, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOBBYN
utterances.text: I was going to move on from this particular topic, unless Your Honours had some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I would like to kick in a question in pursuit of the questions put to you by Mr. Dobbyn, namely, in respect of your testimony that the War Presidencies or war commissions were -- were established where the Crisis Staffs had appeared to function the worst. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the decision on the formation of war commissions, and that's the last of the decisions, the 10th of June. And it says that the commissioner is tasked with getting the municipal organs functioning again. So my understanding is that's where the -- the Municipal Assembly had not been able or didn't look like it was going to be able to meet where the Crisis Staff did not perhaps have -- had not -- did not have an Executive Committee, municipal executive committee. It's not specified in what ways they're not functioning. We see most of the commissions being formed upon this decision in Eastern Bosnian, Birac [Realtime transcript read in error "Bihac"] area is where we first see war commissions formed. They weren't formed everywhere. But the decision is not as extensive as the earlier instructions and it simply says, Republican commissioner is to go where those places where the municipal organs are not functioning. But where we see war commissions actually functioning, where we have documents of them, they are functioning exactly the same as Municipal War Presidencies in Rajlovac, or in Ilidza. They just can't even keep the terminology straight sometimes. It seems to be quite interchangeable. So although the text of the decision on war commissions makes it sound like they are rather a different body, where we see them operating in the documentary evidence, they are operating like a War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that one difference in the way in which Crisis Staffs and war commissions were established was that the war commissions seemed to be tied more closely to the republican level. How was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of the emphasis on the role of the commissioner. We see the commissioner mentioned already in Djeric's instructions of 26 April. The instructions in May are a little more explicit, but again the war commissioner decision -- or decision on formation of war commissions is a shorter, briefer decision but it explains more about the role of the commissioner. And I'm not trying to say that he skips the regional level, it's just that the places where we see war commissions at first are -- we don't see much of a regional Crisis Staff there. I have so little evidence on regional Crisis Staffs outside of the ARK that I can't say -- when I say that he tightens the ties to the republican level, I don't mean to say that he is skipping the regional level, I just don't know what the regional level was doing in those places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. You just told us that the difference was the role of the commissioner. What do you mean by that? Was it the powers he had or was it the way in which he was appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The role was the same. I meant it was the emphasis on him, just the amount of time and the text that is devoted to explaining the role of the commissioner. In Djeric's instructions it's very brief. It's just, Report to the authorities, that is, the republican commissioner. But if you look at the text of the decision on war commissions, it says more about what he should do. It doesn't contradict earlier instructions, it is simply fuller. And therefore I feel it places more emphasis on the commissioner. But always his role is to be the link, the personal link between the republican level and the municipal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So that does suggest somehow a bypassing of the regional level, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I'm very reluctant to make any conclusions about the regional Crisis Staffs as a pattern because of the imbalance in the evidence. But I don't see commissioners in the ARK until much later. I see them -- maybe one or two appointed in some areas that were kind of peripheral to the ARK, but I see them first in Eastern Bosnia where I do not see a strong regional Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And my final question is, was there any difference? Did the appointment of commissioners and war commissions instead of having the Crisis Staffs, did that imply any difference in the way in which the local areas were managed? Did it help?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where I see a war commission functioning, I do not see any difference in its functions between that and of a War Presidency or Crisis Staff, but there's a difference between a commissioner being there and a war commission actually operating. So I do see some reference to the commissioners working well, being effective links, but I don't see that war commissions -- I don't have enough on war commissions operating in places where there hadn't been an effective government before, I don't see that. So it's hard to say that they made a difference or what the difference was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, the situation on the ground in the municipalities didn't change, but did the links between the local level and the republican level improve by virtue of the commissioners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what impacts did this improved correspondence have on the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Better information between the municipal level and the republican, better lines of communication of policy, financial assistance in that they would be able to raise their issues, what they felt needed fixing in their municipality, what they needed money for better. That's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, just before you start there is one intervention in the transcript. I am sorry, I didn't want to disturb the Judge's question. 42 -- page 42, line 23. It says here: "... the commissions being formed upon this decision in Eastern Bosnia, Bihac area ..." There's something because Bihac is Western Bosnia, so if you can please clarify this with the witness, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
